newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: RTRS-PNG hit by looting, soldiers back sacked commander.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-PNG hit by looting, soldiers back sacked commander.

text.p: The capital of Papua New Guinea was hit by looting and lawlessness on Thursday as criminal gangs took advantage of a political crisis and angry soldiers demanded the reinstatement of their sacked commander.
Police fired tear gas against looting raids around the city and rifle shots rang out sporadically near an army barracks that has become the focus for protest against Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan.
The crisis started on Monday when army chief Jerry Singirok demanded that Chan resign for hiring foreign mercenaries to end a conflict on Bougainville island. Singirok was soon sacked.
But Thursday's unrest was criminal as much as political. Local gangs known as "rascals" make Port Moresby one of the world's most dangerous cities even in normal times.
"It's just looting," said a police officer. "People are taking advantage of the situation."

The wider political crisis continued. Senior army officers gave a defence ministry official a petition with 4,700 signatures -- representing virtually all army personnel -- demanding that mander Brigadier-General Jerry Singirok be reinstated within hours.

The petition, which set a deadline of four p.m. (0600 GMT), demanded that all those connected with the mercenary operation stand down and an independent inquiry be set up to investigate the US$28 million contract with British military company Sandline International.
"Everybody down the ranks ... are all in support of the general," an army captain told reporters at the barracks.
But he said soldiers did not intend joining in any street protests, adding: "That would defeat the whole purpose."
Prime Minister Chan signalled a climbdown over the mercenaries on Wednesday. By that time the first six of 40 mercenaries, who are mostly South African, had left the South Pacific nation.
One soldier told reporters at Singapore airport that the contract with Sandline had already been terminated.

British diplomats said they were trying to track down a former U.N. peackeeper who is leading the mercenary group. Tim Spicer, a retired British colonel who was a U.N. military spokesman in Bosnia and now heads Sandline, was believed held by PNG troops on the outskirts of Port Moresby.
Chan and his cabinet met in emergency session on Thursday morning and the prime minister also met three senior Australian officials sent by Prime Minister John Howard.

Howard has condemned any use of mercenaries on Bougainville and proposed alternatives thought to involve more extensive Australian training for the PNG Defence Force. Increased Australian aid could be a way out of the crisis for Chan.
About 2,000 protesters and looters gathered outside the Port Moresby barracks on Thursday morning and police had to fire tear gas to protect a nearby supermarket.

"A security guard inside a building grabbed a hand as it came through and chopped it off," a policeman said after one looting raid. The severed hand was left on a footpath while the looter ran off with his bloodied arm wrapped in a T-shirt.
The crowd grew to around 5,000 before dispersing but large groups continued to roam through the city and police mounted roadblocks at key intersections.
The looters have targeted Chinese shops, reflecting popular resentment against ethnic Chinese businessmen. Chan himself is part-Chinese.
Although it has kept up the pressure on Chan, the army has not joined in any of the street protests.

A senior Singirok aide, Colonel Jack Tuat, was applauded by a crowd of soldiers inside the barracks on Thursday when he told them: "I know you are concerned about the happenings outside, but do not take part...All units, we must appear now at this point of time to be loyal."
